payload.blocks: Only the default value of one new config key. The planner and the implementation go on with no cap (today's behaviour) until you answer; nothing waits.
payload.headline: Cap memory per run supervisor's own systemd scope by default? (8G, none, or 4G)

parts.cause: Checked on fg-server2 (31G RAM): the watcher cgroup peaked at 17.4G with every head inside it; single fgos processes reached 1.4G; a watcher tick uses about 420M; the machine-wide OOM on 2026-11-26 also killed systemd --user. Separate scopes alone fix the shared failure; a cap is what stops one runaway from pushing the whole machine into OOM. The right default is a product choice: a cap that is too low kills a real cargo compile mid-run.

options.cost: Same code for every option: one default value in core/config-standard, about 1 line.
options.does: The new scope memory-cap config key defaults to 8G (MemoryMax); owners can change or empty it in config.
options.gain: A runaway head or worker dies alone at 8G, before a machine-wide OOM that also kills systemd --user.
options.harm: A worker that really needs more than 8G (a very large compile) is killed and its round fails until the key is raised.
options.label: 8G cap per scope

options.does: The key exists and is empty by default; scopes only separate failure domains.
options.gain: Nothing that runs today can be killed by a new limit.
options.harm: One runaway can still fill the 31G and trigger a machine-wide OOM, which may kill systemd --user and everything under it.
options.label: No cap by default

options.gain: Tighter protection; more heads fit side by side.
options.harm: Likely kills real cargo workspace compiles and the larger node children (1.4G measured) plus agent memory.
options.label: 4G cap per scope

parts.recommendation: 8G: separate scopes already fix the shared failure; 8G also stops one runaway from causing a machine-wide OOM while staying far above anything measured (1.4G per process). Until you answer, the change ships with no cap, which is today's behaviour.

scope.allows: Setting the default value of the scope memory-cap config key for every project using fgOS; owners can still override it in project or global config.
scope.forbids: Any change to how scopes are created, which processes get one, the OOM policy, or the watcher's own unit; those are settled in the discussion.

parts.what: Each head's and each run's supervisor will get its own systemd user scope (its own cgroup), so one OOM kill no longer takes the watcher and other heads with it. A scope can also carry a memory ceiling (MemoryMax): above it the kernel kills only inside that scope instead of starting a machine-wide OOM.
